prompt_version: s5-extract-facts-v2 (adapted from Paleo Atlas extract-facts-v3; v2 after Sofía's S5 review)

facts.statement: The study was a retrospective cohort study of newborns with brain injury from oxygen deprivation who were treated with cooling in a specialized neonatal intensive care unit.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The analysis included 106 newborns, split into two groups of 50 and 56 based on which sedation guideline was in use.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The older dosing guideline started at 0.05 micrograms per kilogram per hour and allowed increases of 0.05 micrograms per kilogram per hour every 6 hours.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The newer guideline started at a higher dose of 0.2 micrograms per kilogram per hour and allowed smaller, more frequent adjustments of 0.1 micrograms per kilogram per hour every 30 to 60 minutes.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Doctors followed the new dosing recommendations 69.6% of the time for starting doses, 62.5% for increases, and only 44.6% for decreases.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Newborns in the group using the newer dosing guideline had a higher chance of also receiving opioid painkillers and a higher rate of slow heart rate (21.4% compared to 4%).
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: There were no significant differences between the two groups in how well the sedation worked or in the occurrence of low blood pressure.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The newer dosing method was not linked to better sedation results but was linked to more opioid use and more instances of slow heart rate.
facts.subject: humans
